title: Capital of France
examples: what is the capital of france
capital city of france
where is paris
answer: The capital of France is **Paris**, also its largest city and the country's main cultural and economic centre.

title: Capital of Japan
examples: what is the capital of japan
capital city of japan
is tokyo the capital of japan
answer: The capital of Japan is **Tokyo**, which took over from Kyoto in 1868 and is now one of the largest metropolitan areas in the world.

title: Capital of Australia
examples: what is the capital of australia
capital city of australia
is sydney the capital of australia
answer: The capital of Australia is **Canberra**, not Sydney or Melbourne. It was purpose-built as a compromise between the two rival cities.

title: Capital of Canada
examples: what is the capital of canada
capital city of canada
is toronto the capital
answer: The capital of Canada is **Ottawa**, in Ontario. Toronto is larger, but Ottawa is the seat of the federal government.

title: Capital of Brazil
examples: what is the capital of brazil
capital city of brazil
is rio the capital of brazil
answer: The capital of Brazil is **Brasília**, a planned city built in the 1950s. Rio de Janeiro was the capital before that.

title: Capital of Egypt
examples: what is the capital of egypt
capital city of egypt
answer: The capital of Egypt is **Cairo**, the largest city in the Arab world, sitting on the Nile.

title: Capital of India
examples: what is the capital of india
capital city of india
answer: The capital of India is **New Delhi**, part of the larger Delhi metropolitan area in the north of the country.

title: Capital of Kenya
examples: what is the capital of kenya
capital city of kenya
answer: The capital of Kenya is **Nairobi**, which is also a major regional hub for business and transport in East Africa.

title: Capital of Norway
examples: what is the capital of norway
capital city of norway
answer: The capital of Norway is **Oslo**, on the country's southern coast.

title: Capital of Argentina
examples: what is the capital of argentina
capital city of argentina
answer: The capital of Argentina is **Buenos Aires**, on the Río de la Plata, and home to about a third of the population.

title: Capital of the United States
examples: what is the capital of the usa
capital of the united states
is new york the capital
answer: The capital of the United States is **Washington, D.C.** New York City is bigger, but it is not the capital.

title: Largest country
examples: what is the largest country in the world
biggest country by area
how big is russia
answer: **Russia** is the largest country by area at about 17.1 million square kilometres, roughly 11% of the world's land. Canada is second and China third.

title: Smallest country
examples: what is the smallest country in the world
smallest country by area
answer: **Vatican City** is the smallest country, at about 0.44 square kilometres and roughly 800 residents. Monaco is the second smallest.

title: Longest river
examples: what is the longest river in the world
how long is the nile
is the amazon longer than the nile
casual: nile or amazon which is longer
answer: The **Nile** is usually listed as the longest river at about 6,650 km, with the Amazon close behind at roughly 6,400 km. The Amazon carries far more water.

title: Oceans
examples: what is the largest ocean
how deep is the ocean
what is the deepest ocean
casual: wat is the deepest place in the ocean
answer: The **Pacific** is the largest and deepest ocean, covering about a third of the planet. Its Challenger Deep is roughly 10,900 m down, deeper than Everest is tall.

title: Highest mountain
examples: what is the highest mountain in the world
how tall is mount everest
answer: **Mount Everest** is the highest mountain above sea level at 8,849 m. Measured from base to peak, Mauna Kea in Hawaii is taller.

title: Deserts
examples: what is the largest desert in the world
how big is the sahara
answer: **Antarctica** is the largest desert, because a desert is defined by low precipitation rather than sand. The Sahara is the largest hot desert.

title: Continents
examples: how many continents are there
what are the seven continents
answer: There are **seven** continents: Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe and Australia. Some countries teach six by combining Europe and Asia.

title: World population
examples: what is the world population
how many people are there in the world
answer: The world population passed **8 billion** in 2022 and is still growing, though the rate is slowing. India is now the most populous country, ahead of China.

title: Most spoken languages
examples: what is the most spoken language
how many languages are there
what language has the most native speakers
answer: **Mandarin Chinese** has the most native speakers, around 940 million, while **English** has the most total speakers once second-language users are counted. There are about 7,000 living languages.

title: Time zones
examples: why do we have time zones
how many time zones are there
what is utc
casual: why is there a time difference
answer: Time zones exist because the Sun cannot be overhead everywhere at once. Earth rotates 15 degrees per hour, so the world is divided into 24 nominal zones of one hour each, though real borders make about 38 different offsets. **UTC** is the reference clock; GMT is the older equivalent.

title: Planets
examples: how many planets are there
what is the largest planet
why is pluto not a planet
casual: how many planets in the solar system
answer: There are **eight** planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. **Jupiter** is the largest. Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006 because it has not cleared its orbit of other debris.

title: Distance to the Moon
examples: how far away is the moon
how long does light take from the moon
casual: how far is the moon from earth
answer: The Moon is about **384,400 km** away on average. Light takes roughly 1.3 seconds to cover that, which is why radio commands to the Moon have a noticeable delay.

title: Distance to the Sun
examples: how far away is the sun
how long does sunlight take to reach earth
answer: The Sun is about **150 million km** away, which is one astronomical unit. Sunlight takes about **8 minutes 20 seconds** to reach us, so you always see the Sun as it was eight minutes ago.

title: The Milky Way
examples: what galaxy are we in
how big is the milky way
how many stars are in our galaxy
casual: which galaxy do we live in
answer: We live in the **Milky Way**, a barred spiral galaxy roughly 100,000 light years across with an estimated 100 to 400 billion stars. The nearest large galaxy is Andromeda, about 2.5 million light years away.

title: Nearest star
examples: what is the nearest star to earth
how far is the closest star
answer: The nearest star is the Sun. The nearest star other than the Sun is **Proxima Centauri**, about 4.24 light years away.

title: Why stars twinkle
examples: why do stars twinkle
why do stars flicker at night
answer: Stars twinkle because their light passes through moving layers of atmosphere that bend it slightly, so brightness and position flicker. Planets look steadier because they appear as small discs rather than points.

title: Why Mars is red
examples: why is mars red
what makes mars look red
answer: Mars looks red because its surface dust is rich in **iron oxide**, essentially rust. The dust also fills the thin atmosphere, tinting the sky a butterscotch colour.

title: Saturn's rings
examples: what are saturns rings made of
why does saturn have rings
casual: what are the rings of saturn
answer: Saturn's rings are made of countless pieces of **water ice and rock**, from grains to house-sized chunks. They are probably remnants of a destroyed moon or comet, and they are only tens of metres thick.

title: Bones
examples: how many bones are in the human body
how many bones does an adult have
casual: how many bones do we have
answer: An adult has **206 bones**. Babies are born with roughly 270, and many fuse together as they grow.

title: Heart rate
examples: how many times does the heart beat a day
what is a normal resting heart rate
casual: how many times does ur heart beat
answer: A resting heart rate is typically **60 to 100 beats per minute**, and at about 70 bpm the heart beats roughly 100,000 times a day. Athletes often sit lower, sometimes in the 40s.

title: Blood
examples: how much blood is in the human body
what are the blood types
casual: how much blood do we have
answer: An adult has roughly **5 litres** of blood. Blood types come from the ABO system (A, B, AB, O) plus the Rh factor, giving eight common combinations; O negative is the universal red-cell donor.

title: Body temperature
examples: what is normal body temperature
what counts as a fever
answer: Normal body temperature is about **37°C (98.6°F)**, though healthy people vary by half a degree or so and it dips in the morning. A fever is generally above 38°C.

title: Neurons
examples: how many neurons are in the brain
do we only use 10 percent of our brain
casual: is the 10 percent brain myth true
answer: The brain has roughly **86 billion neurons**, wired through trillions of synapses. The idea that we use only 10% of it is a myth: you use essentially all of your brain, just not all at once.

title: Largest organ
examples: what is the largest organ in the body
how much skin does a person have
answer: The **skin** is the largest organ, about 1.5 to 2 square metres and roughly 15% of body weight. The liver is the largest internal organ.

title: Teeth
examples: how many teeth do adults have
how many baby teeth are there
casual: how many teeth do we have
answer: Adults have **32 teeth** including four wisdom teeth; children have 20 baby teeth. Not everyone develops wisdom teeth, and many people have them removed.

title: Fastest animals
examples: what is the fastest land animal
what is the fastest animal in the world
answer: The **cheetah** is the fastest land animal, reaching about 100 to 120 km/h in short bursts. Overall the **peregrine falcon** wins, exceeding 300 km/h in a dive.

title: Largest animal
examples: what is the largest animal in the world
how big is a blue whale
casual: how long is a blue whale
answer: The **blue whale** is the largest animal known to have lived, around 30 m long and 150 tonnes. Its heart alone can weigh as much as a small car.

title: Octopuses
examples: how many hearts does an octopus have
why is octopus blood blue
answer: An octopus has **three hearts** and blue blood, because it uses copper-based haemocyanin instead of iron-based haemoglobin to carry oxygen. Two hearts pump blood to the gills and one to the body.

title: Giraffes
examples: what is the tallest animal
how tall is a giraffe
answer: The **giraffe** is the tallest living animal, with males reaching about 5.5 m. Its neck has the same seven vertebrae as yours, just much larger ones.

title: Why cats purr
examples: why do cats purr
how do cats purr
answer: Cats purr by rapidly vibrating muscles in the larynx while breathing, producing 25 to 150 Hz. It usually signals contentment, but cats also purr when anxious or in pain, and the vibration may aid healing.

title: Bees and pollination
examples: why are bees important
how do bees pollinate
answer: Bees move pollen between flowers as they feed, which fertilises plants. Roughly a third of the food we eat depends on animal pollination, and honeybees are only one of thousands of pollinating bee species.

title: How much water to drink
examples: how much water should i drink a day
do i need 8 glasses of water
answer: Most adults need roughly **2 to 2.5 litres of fluid a day**, and a good chunk of that comes from food, tea and coffee. Thirst and pale urine are better guides than a fixed number, and needs rise with heat and exercise.

title: Coffee
examples: is coffee bad for you
how much coffee is too much
answer: For most adults, up to about **400 mg of caffeine a day** (roughly three to four cups of coffee) is considered safe. It can disturb sleep and raise anxiety, so the cutoff time matters as much as the amount.

title: Why onions make you cry
examples: why do onions make you cry
how do i stop crying when cutting onions
casual: why do onoins make u cry
answer: Cutting an onion breaks cells and releases enzymes that produce a volatile sulfur compound, which reacts with the water in your eyes to make mild acid. Chilling the onion first slows the reaction, and a sharp knife does less cell damage.

title: Why bread rises
examples: why does bread rise
how does yeast make bread rise
casual: how does yeast work in bread
answer: Yeast eats sugars in the dough and releases **carbon dioxide**, which inflates the gluten network into bubbles. Baking sets that structure, and the steam and gas expand it further before the crust hardens.

title: Boiling and freezing points
examples: what temperature does water boil
what temperature does water freeze
answer: Water boils at **100°C (212°F)** and freezes at **0°C (32°F)** at sea level. At altitude the boiling point drops, which is why cooking takes longer in the mountains.

title: Boiling an egg
examples: how long do i boil an egg
how long to boil a soft boiled egg
answer: About **6 minutes** gives a set white with a runny yolk, 8 minutes a jammy middle, and 10 to 12 minutes a fully hard egg. Start from boiling water and cool them in cold water afterwards.

title: Why bananas ripen
examples: why do bananas ripen so fast
what is ethylene
answer: Bananas release **ethylene** gas, which speeds up ripening in the fruit itself and in anything stored nearby. That is why a ripe banana makes other fruit ripen faster, and why separating them slows it down.

title: Miles and kilometres
examples: how many kilometres are in a mile
convert 10 miles to km
answer: One mile is **1.609 kilometres**, so a 10 km run is about 6.2 miles. A rough rule of thumb is to multiply miles by 1.6.

title: Pounds and kilograms
examples: how many pounds are in a kilogram
convert 70 kg to pounds
casual: how many lbs in a kilo
answer: One kilogram is **2.205 pounds**, and one pound is about 0.45 kg. To go from kg to pounds, roughly double and add 10%.

title: Metres and feet
examples: how many feet are in a metre
convert 1.8 metres to feet
casual: how tall is 180 cm in feet
answer: One metre is **3.281 feet**, so 1.8 m is about 5 feet 11 inches. One foot is 0.3048 m.

title: Gallons and litres
examples: how many litres are in a gallon
convert 5 gallons to litres
answer: One US gallon is **3.785 litres**; an imperial gallon is 4.546 litres. That difference is why fuel economy figures do not match between the US and the UK.

title: Hectares
examples: what is a hectare
how many acres in a hectare
answer: A hectare is **10,000 square metres**, a square 100 m on a side, or about 2.47 acres. It is the standard unit for land area in most of the world.

title: Celsius to Fahrenheit
examples: how do i convert celsius to fahrenheit
what is 20 celsius in fahrenheit
answer: Multiply by 9, divide by 5, then add 32: `F = C × 9/5 + 32`. So 20°C is 68°F, and 37°C is 98.6°F.

title: Bytes and file sizes
examples: how many bytes are in a kilobyte
megabyte vs gigabyte
casual: how many mb in a gb
answer: A kilobyte is 1,000 bytes in SI terms, though operating systems often show 1,024. A megabyte is 1,000 kilobytes and a gigabyte is 1,000 megabytes, so a 1 GB file is a billion bytes.

title: Seconds in a day
examples: how many seconds are in a day
how many minutes in a day
casual: how many hours in a week
answer: A day has **86,400 seconds**: 24 hours, 1,440 minutes. A week is 168 hours, and a year is about 31.5 million seconds.

title: End of World War II
examples: when did world war 2 end
what year did ww2 end
answer: World War II ended in **1945**: Germany surrendered in May, and Japan in August after the atomic bombings and the Soviet declaration of war. The formal surrender was signed on 2 September 1945.

title: The Berlin Wall
examples: when did the berlin wall fall
why was the berlin wall built
casual: when did the wall come down
answer: The Berlin Wall fell in **November 1989** after East Germany opened its borders, and Germany reunified in 1990. It had been built in 1961 to stop people fleeing to the West.

title: The Moon landing
examples: when did humans land on the moon
who was the first person on the moon
answer: Apollo 11 landed on **20 July 1969**, and Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon, followed by Buzz Aldrin. Twelve people have walked on the Moon in total, all between 1969 and 1972.

title: The Titanic
examples: when did the titanic sink
how many people died on the titanic
answer: The Titanic struck an iceberg late on 14 April **1912** and sank early the next morning. About 1,500 of the roughly 2,200 people aboard died, largely because there were too few lifeboats.

title: The printing press
examples: who invented the printing press
when was the printing press invented
answer: Johannes Gutenberg built the movable-type printing press in Europe around **1440**. It made books cheap enough to spread literacy and helped drive the Reformation and the scientific revolution.

title: The French Revolution
examples: when did the french revolution start
what caused the french revolution
answer: The French Revolution began in **1789** with the storming of the Bastille on 14 July. It ended the monarchy, reshaped French society, and led to Napoleon's rise.

title: First US president
examples: who was the first president of the united states
when did george washington become president
answer: **George Washington** was the first US president, taking office in 1789 and serving two terms. He was elected unanimously by the Electoral College both times.

title: Wi-Fi
examples: how does wifi work
what is the difference between 2.4 and 5 ghz
answer: Wi-Fi is radio communication on unlicensed bands, mostly 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz, between your device and an access point. The 2.4 GHz band reaches further but is slower and more crowded; 5 GHz is faster at shorter range.

title: GPS
examples: how does gps work
how does my phone know where i am
casual: how does gps know my location
answer: GPS receivers listen to timing signals from satellites with known orbits. The travel time of each signal gives a distance, and four or more distances pin down your position and the clock error. It is receive-only, so your phone does not transmit to the satellites.

title: Browser cache
examples: what is a browser cache
why do i need to clear my cache
casual: why does clearing cache fix things
answer: The cache is a local store of files the browser already downloaded, so pages load faster. It causes trouble when a site updates but the browser keeps serving an old file, which is why a hard refresh or clearing the cache fixes odd bugs.

title: Why restarting helps
examples: why does restarting fix so many problems
does turning it off and on again work
casual: turn it off and on again
answer: Restarting clears memory that leaked, resets drivers and network state, and ends stuck processes. Most 'turn it off and on again' success comes from resetting state that accumulated into a bad configuration.

title: Phone battery life
examples: why does my phone battery drain so fast
how do i make my battery last longer
casual: why is my battery so bad
answer: The screen, radios and background apps dominate battery use. Lowering brightness, limiting background refresh, and keeping the phone out of extreme heat will do more than most 'battery saver' tricks; heat is what actually wears the cells out.

title: 4G and 5G
examples: what is the difference between 4g and 5g
how does mobile data work
answer: 4G and 5G are generations of mobile data standards. 5G uses wider channels and higher frequencies for more speed and lower latency, but at shorter range, so it needs more cell sites to cover the same area.

title: Credit scores
examples: what is a credit score
how do i improve my credit score
casual: why does my credit score matter
answer: A credit score estimates how reliably you repay debt, based on your history of payments, how much credit you use, and how long you have held accounts. Paying on time and keeping balances low relative to your limits are the two biggest levers.

title: Mortgages
examples: what is a mortgage
how does a mortgage work
answer: A mortgage is a loan secured against a property: the lender can repossess the home if you stop paying. You pay interest plus principal over a fixed term, and a bigger deposit lowers both the rate and the monthly cost.

title: Why the ocean is salty
examples: why is the ocean salty
where does sea salt come from
answer: Rain slightly dissolves rock and carries minerals to the sea, where water evaporates but the salts stay behind. Over hundreds of millions of years this accumulated to about 3.5% salinity.

title: Why plants are green
examples: why is grass green
why are plants green
answer: Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light for photosynthesis but reflects green, so green is the part that reaches your eyes. It is the light the plant does not use.

title: Autumn leaves
examples: why do leaves change colour in autumn
why do leaves turn red and yellow
answer: In autumn, shorter days and cold slow chlorophyll production, so the green fades and the yellows and oranges that were already there become visible. Reds often come from new pigments the tree makes as it withdraws nutrients before dropping the leaf.

title: Magnets
examples: how do magnets work
why do magnets attract metal
answer: Magnetism comes from moving and spinning electric charges. In a magnet, electron spins line up so their fields add, producing a field with a north and south pole. Opposite poles attract, like poles repel, and cutting a magnet just makes two smaller magnets.

title: Why ice is slippery
examples: why is ice slippery
why can you skate on ice
answer: Ice is slippery because a thin, mobile layer of water molecules sits on its surface even well below freezing. Pressure and friction add a little more melt, which is why skates glide, but the surface layer does most of the work.

title: Goosebumps
examples: why do we get goosebumps
what causes goosebumps
casual: why do i get goosebumps when cold
answer: Tiny muscles at the base of each hair contract, lifting the hair and dimpling the skin. It is a leftover reflex for trapping warmth and looking bigger, and it still fires with cold or strong emotion.

title: Dreams
examples: why do we dream
what do dreams mean
answer: Dreams happen mostly in REM sleep, when the brain is highly active while the body is paralysed. The leading explanations are memory consolidation and emotional processing; there is no good evidence that dreams predict the future or carry coded messages.

title: The 10% brain myth
examples: do we only use 10 percent of our brain
is the 10 percent brain myth true
casual: how much of our brain do we use
answer: The claim that we use only 10% of our brain is false. Imaging shows activity across the whole brain over a day, and damage to almost any area causes problems. The myth survives because it is flattering and simple.

title: The smell of rain
examples: why does rain smell so good
what is petrichor
casual: why does it smell after rain
answer: That scent is called **petrichor**. Rain hits soil and releases oils from plants plus a compound made by soil bacteria, and the drops also trap and carry airborne molecules into your nose.

title: Fireflies
examples: why do fireflies glow
how do fireflies make light
answer: Fireflies produce light through a chemical reaction between luciferin and oxygen, catalysed by an enzyme, which releases almost no heat. The flashes are mainly courtship signals, and each species has its own pattern.

title: Yawning
examples: why do we yawn
why is yawning contagious
answer: Yawning probably helps regulate brain temperature and alertness, though the exact purpose is still debated. Contagious yawning is real and is linked to empathy; it appears in humans and some other primates.

title: Why space is dark
examples: why is space dark
why is it black in space
answer: Space looks black because it is almost empty, so there is nothing to scatter light toward your eyes. The night sky is also dark because the universe has a finite age, so light from the most distant stars has not reached us yet.

title: Thunder and lightning
examples: why is there thunder after lightning
how do i tell how far away lightning is
casual: how far is lightning if i count seconds
answer: Lightning heats the air to about 30,000°C in a fraction of a second, and the air expands explosively, producing thunder. Count the seconds between flash and boom and divide by three to get the distance in kilometres.

title: Rainbows
examples: how does a rainbow form
why are rainbows curved
answer: Sunlight entering a raindrop refracts, reflects off the back and refracts again, splitting into colours at about 42 degrees from the direction opposite the Sun. A rainbow is actually a full circle; the ground hides the lower half.

title: Hot air balloons
examples: how do hot air balloons work
why do hot air balloons float
answer: Heating the air inside the envelope makes it less dense than the cooler air outside, so it rises, much like a bubble in water. The pilot controls altitude by heating or letting the air cool.

title: How planes fly
examples: how do airplanes fly
what keeps a plane in the air
casual: how does a plane stay up
answer: Wings generate **lift** by turning the airflow downward. The curved shape and the angle of the wing accelerate air over the top and deflect it down, and by Newton's third law the wing is pushed up. It is not simply that air has to travel faster over the top.

title: Radio
examples: how does radio work
what is the difference between am and fm
answer: Radio carries information on electromagnetic waves far below visible light. AM varies the strength of the wave, which survives distance but picks up noise; FM varies its frequency, which sounds cleaner but needs a stronger signal.

title: How soap works
examples: how does soap clean
why does soap kill viruses
casual: why is soap better than water
answer: Soap molecules have a water-loving end and a fat-loving end, so they surround oils and dirt and let water rinse them away. They also break apart the fatty outer layer of many viruses. Friction and 20 seconds of scrubbing matter as much as the soap.

title: Herd immunity
examples: what is herd immunity
why does vaccination protect others
answer: Herd immunity is when enough people are immune that the pathogen cannot find new hosts easily, so outbreaks fizzle out. The threshold differs by disease and is higher for measles, which is extremely contagious.

title: Sunscreen
examples: what does spf mean
how does sunscreen work
answer: SPF mostly measures protection from UVB, the burning rays: SPF 30 blocks about 97% of UVB versus 93% for SPF 15. You still need UVA protection, and reapplication matters more than a high number because sweat and rubbing remove it.

title: Sugar in drinks
examples: how much sugar is in a can of soda
is juice as bad as soda
casual: how much sugar in soft drinks
answer: A standard 330 ml can of cola has about **35 g of sugar**, roughly seven teaspoons, and around 140 calories. Fruit juice is similar in sugar, just with a different vitamin profile.

title: Why food spoils
examples: why does food go bad
how does a fridge keep food fresh
casual: how does refrigeration work for food
answer: Food spoils because bacteria, moulds and enzymes break it down, and their growth is fastest in warmth and moisture. Refrigeration slows them, salt and acid inhibit them, and canning removes the oxygen they need.

title: Speed and distance
examples: how far do you travel at 100 kmh in an hour
convert 100 kmh to mph
answer: At 100 km/h you cover 100 km in an hour, so speed is simply distance divided by time. 100 km/h is about 62 mph; multiply km/h by 0.62 for mph.

title: Dog years
examples: how do dog years work
is one dog year seven human years
casual: how old is my dog in human years
answer: The seven-to-one rule is a rough myth. Dogs mature much faster early on, so the first year is roughly 15 human years, the second about 9 more, and after that it depends heavily on size: small dogs age more slowly than large ones.

title: Sleep cycles
examples: how long is a sleep cycle
what is rem sleep
answer: A sleep cycle lasts about **90 minutes** and moves through light sleep, deep sleep and REM. Deep sleep dominates early in the night and REM later, which is why a short night cuts REM more than deep sleep.

title: Cold showers
examples: are cold showers good for you
what does a cold shower do
answer: Cold water makes you alert and can lift mood for a while, and it is safe for most healthy people. Claims about fat loss or immunity are much weaker than the marketing suggests; the main benefit is that it wakes you up.

title: Stretching
examples: should i stretch before exercise
does stretching prevent injury
answer: Dynamic movement before exercise warms you up better than long static holds, which can slightly reduce power if done immediately before. Static stretching is most useful afterwards or as its own session for flexibility.

title: Caffeine and sleep
examples: how long does caffeine stay in your body
does coffee affect sleep
answer: Caffeine has a half-life of about **5 hours**, and up to 6 or more in some people, so an afternoon coffee is still partly active at bedtime. It also reduces deep sleep even when you fall asleep fine.

title: Sitting all day
examples: is sitting all day bad for you
how do i fix back pain from sitting
casual: how to survive a desk job
answer: Long uninterrupted sitting is linked to back and neck trouble and worse metabolic health. The fix is frequent movement rather than a perfect posture: stand or walk for a few minutes every half hour and vary how you sit.

title: Headphone volume and hearing
examples: how loud is too loud for headphones
can headphones damage my hearing
answer: Sustained exposure above about **85 decibels** risks hearing damage, and earbuds at high volume easily exceed that. The practical rule is the 60/60 one: no more than 60% volume for no more than 60 minutes at a time.

title: Left-handedness
examples: why are some people left handed
what percentage of people are left handed
answer: About **10%** of people are left-handed. Handedness comes from a mix of genetics and early development rather than a single gene, and it is not a sign of anything else about intelligence.

title: Hiccups
examples: what causes hiccups
how do i stop hiccups
casual: how to get rid of hicups
answer: Hiccups are involuntary spasms of the diaphragm followed by a sudden closure of the vocal cords. They usually stop on their own; slow breathing, sipping water or holding your breath can interrupt the cycle.

title: Sneezing
examples: why do we sneeze
why do we close our eyes when we sneeze
casual: can you sneeze with eyes open
answer: A sneeze clears irritants from the nasal passages, triggered by nerves in the nose. Most people close their eyes reflexively, but nothing bursts if you keep them open; the pressure simply takes another path.

title: Food and concentration
examples: what should i eat to focus better
does breakfast help concentration
answer: Stable blood sugar helps attention, so meals with protein, fibre and slow carbohydrates beat a sugar spike. Hydration matters too: mild dehydration reliably worsens concentration and mood before you feel thirsty.

title: Tallest building
examples: what is the tallest building in the world
how tall is the burj khalifa
casual: how tall is the tallest skyscraper
answer: The **Burj Khalifa** in Dubai is the tallest building at **828 metres** with 163 floors. It has held the record since 2010.

title: Largest island
examples: what is the largest island in the world
is australia an island
casual: why is australia not an island
answer: **Greenland** is the largest island, at about 2.2 million square kilometres. Australia is larger but is classed as a continent rather than an island, which is a convention more than a physical rule.

title: Number of countries
examples: how many countries are there in the world
how many countries are in the un
answer: The usual figure is **195**: 193 member states of the United Nations plus two observer states, the Vatican and Palestine. Some territories and disputed regions are counted differently, which is why you also see numbers like 193 or 197.

title: Roman numerals
examples: how do roman numerals work
what is x in roman numerals
how do i read roman numerals
casual: what does iv mean in roman numerals
how to write 2024 in roman numerals
answer: Roman numerals use **I = 1, V = 5, X = 10, L = 50, C = 100, D = 500, M = 1,000**. Symbols are added left to right, except when a smaller symbol comes before a larger one: IV is 4, IX is 9, XL is 40, and CM is 900. So 2024 is MMXXIV.

title: Binary numbers
examples: how does binary work
what is binary
how do computers count
answer: Binary is base 2: each place is worth twice the one to its right, using only 0 and 1. So **1011** means 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = **11**. Computers use it because a switch has two reliable states, on and off, which is far easier to build and detect than ten distinct voltage levels.

title: Pi
examples: what is pi
what is the value of pi
why is pi important
casual: how many digits of pi are there
answer: **Pi** is the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, about **3.14159**. It appears wherever circles, waves or rotations do. It is irrational, so its decimal never ends or repeats; for almost any real calculation, a handful of digits is plenty.

title: Golden ratio
examples: what is the golden ratio
what is 1.618
is the golden ratio in nature
casual: whats the golden ratio used for
answer: The **golden ratio** is about **1.618**, the proportion where the whole relates to the larger part as the larger part relates to the smaller. It is the limit of ratios of consecutive Fibonacci numbers. Claims that it explains all of art and nature are often exaggerated, but it genuinely shows up in some growth patterns and tilings.

title: Speed of sound
examples: what is the speed of sound
how fast does sound travel
what is mach 1
casual: why do i see lightning before thunder
answer: Sound travels at about **343 metres per second** in air at 20 °C, roughly 1,235 km/h. It moves faster in water and much faster in steel, because the particles are packed closer. Mach 1 means the speed of sound; the delay between lightning and thunder is the same difference, about three seconds per kilometre.

title: Light-year
examples: what is a light year
how far is a light year
is a light year a measure of time
casual: how many km in a light year
why is a light year called a year
answer: A **light-year** is a distance, not a time: the distance light travels in one year, about **9.46 trillion kilometres**. Astronomers use it because space is huge and kilometres become unwieldy. The nearest star beyond the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.2 light-years away.

title: Absolute zero
examples: what is absolute zero
how cold can it get
what is zero kelvin in celsius
casual: why can nothing be colder than absolute zero
answer: Absolute zero is **-273.15 °C**, or 0 kelvin, the point where a system has the least possible thermal energy. You cannot reach it exactly: cooling something requires removing heat, and the closer you get, the harder the last bit is to remove. Particles still have quantum zero-point motion at that temperature.

title: Size of the Earth
examples: what is the circumference of the earth
how big is the earth
what is the diameter of earth
answer: Earth's circumference around the equator is about **40,075 km**, and its mean diameter is about **12,742 km**. It bulges slightly at the equator because of rotation, so the polar diameter is about 43 km smaller.

title: Auroras
examples: what causes the northern lights
what is an aurora
why are auroras green
casual: where can i see the northern lights
why is the aurora green and purple
answer: Charged particles from the Sun stream toward Earth and are funnelled by the magnetic field toward the poles. There they collide with gas in the upper atmosphere, exciting it, and the gas releases the energy as light. **Oxygen** glows green and red; **nitrogen** gives blue and purple. Auroras are strongest near the poles and during high solar activity.

title: Meteor showers
examples: what causes a meteor shower
what is a shooting star
when is the next meteor shower
answer: A meteor shower happens when Earth passes through debris left by a comet or asteroid. The grains hit the atmosphere at tens of kilometres per second, heat up and burn, and we see a streak. A **shooting star** is not a star at all, just a small piece of rock or dust.

title: The North Star
examples: what is the north star
how do i find the north star
is polaris the brightest star
casual: is the north star the brightest
answer: **Polaris** sits almost directly above Earth's north pole, so it barely moves while the rest of the sky rotates around it. That makes it useful for finding north in the northern hemisphere. It is not the brightest star, only about the 48th, and it is a multiple star system about 430 light-years away.

title: Déjà vu
examples: what causes deja vu
what is deja vu
why do i get deja vu
answer: Déjà vu is the strong feeling that a new situation has happened before, without being able to place it. The leading explanations involve a brief mismatch in memory processing, where familiarity is triggered without the recollection that normally goes with it. It is common, especially when tired, and usually harmless; frequent episodes alongside other symptoms are worth a doctor's opinion.

title: Muscle memory
examples: what is muscle memory
how does muscle memory work
why can i still ride a bike
casual: is muscle memory in the muscles
answer: **Muscle memory** is motor learning, not memory stored in muscle. Repeated practice builds and prunes connections in the brain, especially the cerebellum and motor cortex, so a movement becomes automatic and needs less conscious attention. The muscles change too, but the skill itself lives in the nervous system, which is why it comes back quickly after a long break.

title: Shivering
examples: why do we shiver when cold
what causes shivering
why do i shiver when i have a fever
casual: why do i shake when im cold
answer: Shivering is rapid, involuntary muscle contraction that produces heat as a by-product, a way for the body to defend its core temperature. It is triggered when the hypothalamus decides you are losing heat too fast. With a fever, the set point rises, so you feel cold and shiver until the body reaches the new target.

title: Vitamin D
examples: how do i get vitamin d
what does vitamin d do
how much sun do i need for vitamin d
casual: do i need vitamin d supplements in winter
answer: Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium and is needed for healthy bones and muscles. Skin makes it from **UVB sunlight**, and only a few foods contain much. People with dark skin, little sun exposure or who cover up are more likely to be low; a blood test is the way to know, and supplements should be dosed sensibly rather than guessed at large amounts.

title: Vitamin C
examples: what does vitamin c do
what foods have vitamin c
does vitamin c prevent colds
casual: how much vitamin c do i need
answer: Vitamin C is needed to build collagen, the protein in skin, blood vessels and bone, and it helps the body absorb iron. A severe lack causes **scurvy**, with bleeding gums and slow healing. Citrus, peppers, broccoli and kiwi are rich sources. For most people it does not prevent colds, though it may slightly shorten one.

title: Allergies
examples: what causes allergies
why do i sneeze in spring
how do antihistamines work
casual: why am i allergic to pollen
answer: An allergy is the immune system treating a harmless protein, such as pollen or peanut protein, as a threat. It produces **IgE** antibodies, and the next exposure triggers cells to release **histamine**, causing sneezing, itching, swelling or wheezing. Antihistamines block histamine receptors and reduce the symptoms. Some childhood allergies fade, others persist, and severe reactions need urgent medical help.

title: Viruses and bacteria
examples: what is the difference between a virus and a bacteria
do antibiotics kill viruses
are viruses alive
casual: why dont antibiotics work on a cold
answer: Bacteria are single-celled organisms that can live and reproduce on their own, and most are harmless or useful. Viruses are much smaller packages of genetic material that need a host cell to copy themselves. **Antibiotics** target bacterial machinery, so they do nothing against viruses. That is why a cold, which is usually viral, does not improve with antibiotics.

title: The common cold
examples: how do i get rid of a cold fast
how long does a cold last
is there a cure for the common cold
casual: why do colds last so long
answer: Colds are caused by many different viruses, most often **rhinoviruses**, which is why there is no single vaccine or cure. Symptoms usually peak in two to three days and clear within about a week to ten. Rest, fluids and simple symptom relief help; antibiotics do not. See a doctor if symptoms last much longer, or if breathing becomes difficult.

title: Fever
examples: what is a normal body temperature
is a fever dangerous
should i treat a fever
casual: how to bring down a fever
answer: A fever is a raised body temperature, usually above about **38 °C**, and it is a controlled response that makes it harder for some germs to multiply. Normal temperature varies by person and time of day. A mild fever is often best left to do its job with fluids and rest; babies, pregnant people and anyone with a very high or persistent fever should get medical advice.

title: Alcohol and sleep
examples: does alcohol help you sleep
why do i wake up after drinking
how does alcohol affect sleep
casual: why is sleep bad after drinking
answer: Alcohol can make you fall asleep faster, which is why it feels like a nightcap helps, but it fragments sleep later in the night and suppresses **REM** sleep. It also relaxes the muscles of the airway, worsening snoring and sleep apnoea. The result is a shorter, lighter night even when the total hours look fine.

title: Screens before bed
examples: do screens before bed affect sleep
is blue light bad before bed
how do i stop using my phone at night
casual: why cant i sleep after scrolling
answer: Screens affect sleep two ways: the content keeps your attention and delays bedtime, and bright light near the eyes can shift the body clock. Blue-light filters reduce one part but do not fix the arousal from messages, games or videos. The reliable fix is putting the phone out of reach for the last 30 to 60 minutes before bed.

title: Napping
examples: how long should a nap be
is napping good for you
when should i take a nap
casual: how long is a good nap
why do i feel groggy after a nap
answer: A **10 to 20 minute** nap improves alertness without grogginess. Longer naps let you enter deep sleep, and waking from that leaves sleep inertia for a while. Early afternoon is the easiest time to nap because of a natural dip in alertness; napping late in the day can make it harder to fall asleep at night.

title: Daily steps
examples: do i need 10,000 steps a day
how many steps should i walk
is walking enough exercise
casual: how many steps a day is healthy
answer: The 10,000 figure started as a marketing number, not a medical threshold. Large studies link lower mortality with walking, with benefits rising up to roughly **7,000 to 8,000 steps a day** and flattening after that. Any increase from a very low baseline helps, and brisk walking counts more than a slow stroll.

title: Muscle soreness
examples: why are my muscles sore after exercise
how long does muscle soreness last
is soreness a sign of a good workout
casual: why am i sore two days later
does lactic acid make you sore
answer: Delayed onset muscle soreness usually peaks **24 to 72 hours** after unfamiliar or intense exercise. It comes from microscopic damage and the repair response, not from lactic acid, which clears within hours. Soreness is not a reliable measure of a good session; light movement, sleep and protein help recovery, and sharp pain during exercise is a reason to stop.

title: Emergency fund
examples: how big should my emergency fund be
what is an emergency fund
where should i keep my emergency savings
casual: how much savings should i have
why do i need an emergency fund
answer: An emergency fund covers essential expenses if income stops or a large unexpected bill lands. The common target is **three to six months** of necessities, more if your income is irregular or you support others. Keep it somewhere safe and easy to reach, such as a savings account, rather than in investments that can fall just when you need them.

title: Email etiquette
examples: how do i write a good email
what should an email subject line say
how long should a work email be
casual: how to write a professional email
how to ask for something by email
answer: Put the ask in the subject line or the first sentence, keep the body to a few short paragraphs, and make the next action obvious. One email should carry one request. Reply within a working day when you can, use reply-all sparingly, and avoid sarcasm that text cannot carry. If a thread has gone back and forth more than twice, a short call usually saves time.

title: HTTP status codes
examples: what does a 404 mean
what is the difference between 400 and 500
what are http status codes
casual: why do i get a 500 error
answer: HTTP status codes group by first digit: **2xx** success, **3xx** redirect, **4xx** the client's request is wrong, **5xx** the server failed. Common ones: 200 OK, 301 moved permanently, 400 bad request, 401 not authenticated, 403 forbidden, 404 not found, 429 too many requests, 500 internal error. A 400 means fix the request; a 500 means the server should be fixed.

title: null and undefined
examples: what is the difference between null and undefined
should i use null or undefined in javascript
answer: In JavaScript, **undefined** usually means a value was never assigned, and it is what you get from a missing property or an omitted argument. **null** is an explicit "no value" that a programmer sets on purpose. `typeof null` returning `'object'` is a long-standing bug kept for compatibility. TypeScript's strict null checks make the distinction useful rather than annoying.

title: Flexbox and grid
examples: what is the difference between flexbox and grid
should i use flexbox or grid
how do i choose a css layout
answer: **Flexbox** lays items out along one axis, a row or a column, and is best for a toolbar, a card's internal layout or distributing space between items. **Grid** defines rows and columns at the same time, and is best for page-level layouts and anything that needs alignment in two directions. They compose well: use grid for the page and flexbox inside the components.

title: SQL joins
examples: what is the difference between inner join and left join
how do sql joins work
what is a full outer join
answer: A join combines rows from two tables on a matching condition. **INNER JOIN** keeps only rows with a match in both tables. **LEFT JOIN** keeps every row from the left table and fills unmatched right columns with null; **RIGHT JOIN** is the mirror. **FULL OUTER JOIN** keeps unmatched rows from both sides. Most reporting bugs come from an inner join silently dropping rows you expected to keep.

title: Database indexes
examples: what is a database index
why do indexes make queries faster
why not index every column
casual: how do indexes work in sql
answer: An index is a sorted side structure, usually a **B-tree**, that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table. Reads that filter or sort on the indexed column get much faster. The cost is space and slower writes, because every insert, update and delete must update the index too, so index the columns you actually query rather than everything.

title: API key safety
examples: where should i store an api key
can i put an api key in frontend code
how do i keep secrets safe
casual: is it ok to put api keys in javascript
why are secrets in frontend bad
answer: Anything shipped to a browser can be read, so an API key in frontend code or a public repository is already leaked. Keep keys on the server, load them from environment variables or a secret store, and give each one the narrowest scope possible. If a key has been exposed, rotate it rather than hoping nobody noticed; bots scan public repositories within minutes.

title: Two-factor authentication
examples: what is two factor authentication
why should i use 2fa
is sms 2fa safe
casual: how does two factor auth work
answer: Two-factor authentication asks for something you know, like a password, plus something you have or are, like a code from an app or a security key. That means a stolen password alone is not enough. Authenticator apps and hardware keys are safer than SMS, which can be intercepted or hijacked through SIM swapping, but any second factor beats none.

title: VPNs
examples: what does a vpn do
does a vpn make me anonymous
should i use a vpn on public wifi
answer: A VPN encrypts traffic between your device and the VPN server, so your local network and internet provider cannot read it or see which sites you visit. It does not make you anonymous: the VPN provider can see your traffic, and sites still recognise logins, cookies and browser fingerprints. It is most useful on untrusted networks and for hiding traffic from a local network operator.

title: Browser cookies
examples: what are browser cookies
what is the difference between session and persistent cookies
are cookies bad
casual: why do websites ask about cookies
answer: A cookie is a small piece of data a site asks your browser to store and send back on later requests. **Session cookies** disappear when the browser closes and keep you logged in; **persistent cookies** have an expiry and remember preferences. First-party cookies are usually functional, while third-party tracking cookies are the ones privacy rules target. Blocking all cookies tends to break logins and carts.

title: Parts of a URL
examples: what are the parts of a url
what is a query string in a url
what does https mean in a url
casual: what is the bit after the question mark in a url
what is a fragment in a url
answer: A URL has a **scheme** (`https`), a **host** (`example.com`), an optional **port**, a **path** (`/blog/post`), an optional **query string** (`?page=2&sort=new`) and an optional **fragment** (`#section`) that points inside the page. The query string is data sent to the server; the fragment is handled by the browser and never sent in the request.

title: Backups
examples: how should i back up my files
what is the 3-2-1 backup rule
how often should i back up
casual: how to not lose my files
answer: The **3-2-1 rule** is a good default: keep three copies of important data, on two different kinds of media, with one copy off-site. A backup you have never restored is only a hope, so test a restore occasionally. Synchronising to a cloud drive is not a full backup, because a deletion or ransomware infection gets synced too.

title: Git merge and rebase
examples: what is the difference between merge and rebase
should i merge or rebase
what does git rebase do
answer: **Merge** joins two branches and keeps the real history, adding a merge commit. **Rebase** replays your commits on top of another branch, producing a straight line, but it rewrites commit hashes. Rebase your own local branch before sharing it; once commits are pushed and others may have built on them, merge instead, or you will force everyone to reconcile rewritten history.

title: Semantic versioning
examples: how does semantic versioning work
what does 1.2.3 mean in a version number
what is a major version bump
casual: what does the version number mean
why do versions have three numbers
answer: Semantic versioning uses **major.minor.patch**. Patch increases for backward-compatible bug fixes, minor for backward-compatible features, and major for breaking changes. A version like `2.4.1` is therefore the second major line, fourth feature release, first patch. Pre-release labels such as `3.0.0-beta.1` sort before the final release.
